newsitem.title: GERMANY: Welteke - Bonn could end row by dropping payout call.
newsitem.headline: Welteke - Bonn could end row by dropping payout call.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke was reported on Friday as saying one way out of the dispute with Bonn over planned gold revaluation would be for the government to drop its demand for a payout of a special profit and leave the matter to the Bundesbank.

Welteke was also reported as saying in an interview with Sueddeutsche Zeitung that it was "nonsense" that an overshoot of the three percent reference level for the budget deficit disqualified a nation from joining monetary union.

Welteke said that while the Bundesbank did not have any formal instruments to defend itself against the Bonn government plans, members of parliament should nevertheless take note that the population's confidence in the transition to the planned Euro stemmed from the Bundesbank, not from politicians.
"They should take care that no political damage is done here," Welteke was quoted as saying.

Welteke suggested allowing the Bundesbank's gold and currency reserves to be revalued but dropping the passage requiring a payout of the valuation gain from upcoming amendments to Bundesbank legislation.
The remainder of the amendments could take effect with the launch of monetary union, Welteke said.

The revaluation is necessary in any case as part of preparations for the working of the European central bank but Bonn plans to require the Bundesbank to pay a special profit from the revaluation in several tranches in 1997 and 1998.
The Bundesbank on Wednesday issued a strongly worded statement condemning the move as potentially undermining confidence in the planned single European currency.
Welteke called on Finance Minister Theo Waigel to read the Maastricht Treaty carefully, Sueddeutsche Zeitung said.

He noted that Waigel's CSU party, the sister party to Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats, had decided at its conference that an overshoot of the three percent deficit criterion ruled out membership of the euro.
"That is nonsense in every respect," Welteke said.
The Maastricht Treaty states says a nation's deficit must be no higher than three percent of its gross domestic product (GDP) but the Treaty allows exceptions.
Welteke said there were four areas of disagreement between the Bundesbank and Bonn.

Firstly, Waigel's plan ran counter to current planning of the European Monetary Institute (EMI) -- forerunner to the European central bank -- to transfer valuation gains to a reserve rather than paying them out.
Secondly, commercial banks may also be tempted into accounting tricks if a special exception was allowed for the Bundesbank's accounting methods.
Thirdly, the Bundesbank regarded the request for a revaluation and payout as an intrusion into its independence.
And finally, Bonn was only resorting to the revaluation because it was afraid of failing to meet the Maastricht criteria, Welteke said.
